body:
An interesting delivery of a corporal rehabilitation story that purposefully sprinkles a bunch of incomplete details.

Who is Charlie. We never explicitly are told. Is he a lost elder child of the family?

How was he lost? We see scratched grafitti on the desk, which we're told is second hand.

Chris tells us honestly no one else was ever tied up in that room.

Both parents watch Tommy watch the videos he's posted of his abuse of others. Was one of his victims their son and lost to the fall out of Tommy's abuse. Ie you took our son, now you replace him? It's never answered but it is definitely purposefully outlined, and purposefully left unanswered so it was a story point not to tell us but to let us guess so our incomplete story feeling is meant to be like that, we're meant to be left to fill in thegaps ourselves and it doesn't really matter how we do it.

Ther applying of the wig was another detail that was supposed to mean something yet we're not given the details to finish the thought.

And the girls family saying "I'm here to take my Lump". What ever that means. Never addresssed or explained.

Director Jan Komasa has included multiple examples of this in the film so it's meant to be like that and it does force the view to think, to try and answer these questions and interpret meanings themselves.

It's an interesting technique, which doesn't necessarily work perfectly, but doesn't necessarily distract from the experience enough to damage it either. We're used to stories spelled out for us and then summed up at the end, so it's interesting to see a story play with us a little. We're set up to believe that chris is a dodgy serial type guy applying his toupe, and keeping people in his basement, but, that's not the case, That Kathryn is a sickly domineering heartless damaged figure, but that's not the case, That Jonathan is a damaged kid held prisioner by deranged parents, but again, not the case, so the movie plays with us.

Things aren't clear and there isn't always an easy answer.

In edgy Brit-drama "Heel" (aka "Good Boy") vile anti-social yob Anson Boon (good) is snatched by odd Stephen Graham (strong again) who imprisons him in the basement of the isolated home he shares with equally odd wife Andrea Riseborough, young son Kit Rakusen, & maid Monica Frajczyk - as a well intentioned but def'ly strange project he & Riseborough are running. Jan Komasa directs solidly enough (for his first English language film (before making the mediocre "Anniversary")) but of key interest are co-writers Naqqash Khalid (with his 2nd screenplay) & Bartek Bartosik (on his debut) who are original but morally dubious (and leave some holes). It's imperfect but engaging.

It's a funny old film this. I spent most of it wondering if there was more going on than was apparent. Although it finished with a couple of deliberate loose ends it seems that basically the plot was simply what I'd been looking at all along.

I suppose I'm a bit of a cynic but there was a transformation here which I was able to swallow but which, objectively, might seem a little implausible.

Heel (aka Good Boy) is beautiful and heartfelt, as if it existed on a coin on the other side of Rent A Family. This is not a horror, but rather a drama wrapped in a thriller with a bold premise with a strong emotional payoff.

Anchored in beautiful performances from every-single-actor, accentuated by never-too-slow pace and masterful direction, the film takes you for a ride with unexpected turns, sometimes with a destination you see from miles away, yet still enjoy getting there.

From first shot to last, the story centers on Tommy and his journey, everything else around him is a solid concept with elegant execution.

Visually compelling but not overstated, scored with kindness, and some well crafted dynamics and character relationships, Heel never tries to answer too much, while it keeps you guessing it definitely does not try to wrap everything in a tight neat package.

It is perhaps not a film that will keep my head trying to find answers, rather will stay as an emotional beat in what I consider an exploration of what family really means, for the better or the worse.

If you are looking for an engaging watch that might sway you from "disturbing" to "almost feels good" kind of film, a film that respects your intellect and seeks your emotional buy-in, this is definitely for you.

Last night's 'Secret Screening' was UK/Polish thriller "The Good Boy". I was very happy as this was one of those occasions where I knew absolutely nothing about the film going in, not seen a trailer, nor even a poster. I enjoyed what I saw quite a bit.

Rina (Monika Frajczyk) an Eastern European working in England, is gently coerced into a cleaning job at the large, isolated house belonging to Chris (Stephen Graham). The household includes Chris' wife, the near catatonic Kathryn (Andrea Riseborough), their nervous son Jonathan (Kit Rakusen) and Tommy (Anson Boon) a young man, with a hellraising past, who is chained up in the basement.

To say again, I really liked coming to the film blind, as it's such a rarity for me to have that. It worked for this film particularly, because it's a bit of a genre mix. Mostly it's a thriller. There are shifting sympathies across the run between Tommy and Chris - every time we start to feel bad for Tommy, we (and he, in a "Clockwork Orange" like moment) are shown some form of debauchery, or self-recorded crime to remind us how awful he was. As the film goes on, and Tommy seems more accustomed to his circumstances the internal debate is how safe the family are around him, or whether - like the dog he's been treated like - he might still snap. There are moments of humour though, not enough, for me, to consider the film a black comedy though, as I've seen it classified.

Performances are great. Graham and Riseborough always are. I really like Anson Boon, who was Johnny Rotten in the Sex Pistols bio-show and was in "Mobland" last year - and presumably will be again when it returns. The young kid, Kit Rakusen, is also excellent and some of his facial work - masking fear - is exceptional.

I don't think the ending undermines the earlier film, as I've seen in some professional reviews and indeed the film ends in the only real way I thought it could.

Good stuff.
